name: Hydrogen
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [1.007 84, 1.008 11]
summary: The lightest and most abundant element in the universe, a diatomic gas on Earth. It fuels stars through fusion and sits at the heart of water and all organic chemistry.

name: Helium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
discovered_note: Seen in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 (Janssen, Lockyer); isolated on Earth in 1895 (Ramsay).
summary: A chemically inert noble gas, second lightest element, produced by fusion in stars and by radioactive decay underground. It stays liquid down to absolute zero at normal pressure.

name: Lithium
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [6.938, 6.997]
summary: The lightest metal, soft enough to cut with a knife and reactive in air. It is the key ingredient in rechargeable batteries.

name: Beryllium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 5
summary: A light, stiff, brittle gray metal whose compounds are toxic. Its transparency to X-rays and its stiffness make it useful in precision instruments and windows.

name: Boron
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [10.806, 10.821]
summary: A hard metalloid that forms strong, light compounds with many elements. Borates go into glass, detergents and fertilizers, and it is a trace nutrient for plants.

name: Carbon
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [12.0096, 12.0116]
summary: The backbone of life, able to form long chains and rings with itself. Pure forms include soft graphite, hard diamond and graphene sheets.

name: Nitrogen
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [14.006 43, 14.007 28]
summary: A colorless, mostly inert diatomic gas making up about 78% of air. Fixed into ammonia and nitrates, it becomes essential to proteins and DNA.

name: Oxygen
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [15.999 03, 15.999 77]
summary: A reactive gas that makes up about a fifth of the atmosphere and powers respiration and combustion. It is also the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass, mostly in oxides and silicates.

name: Fluorine
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 5
discovered_note: Isolated by Moissan in 1886; fluorspar and its acid were known earlier.
summary: The most electronegative and reactive element, a pale yellow gas that attacks almost everything. Its compounds appear in toothpaste, nonstick coatings and refrigerants.

name: Neon
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 6
summary: A colorless noble gas that glows orange-red in discharge tubes. It forms essentially no stable compounds.

name: Sodium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A soft, silvery metal that reacts vigorously with water. Its ion is vital for nerve signals and it makes up common salt with chlorine.

name: Magnesium
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [24.304, 24.307]
summary: A light, silvery metal that burns with a dazzling white flame. It sits at the center of chlorophyll and is an important ion in cells.

name: Aluminum
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A light, corrosion-resistant metal and the most abundant metal in Earth's crust. It is mostly extracted from bauxite and used in aircraft, cans and cables.

name: Silicon
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [28.084, 28.086]
summary: A shiny metalloid and the base of most rocks, sand and glass. Purified crystals form the semiconductor chips of modern electronics.

name: Phosphorus
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 5
summary: A reactive nonmetal that appears as white, red or black allotropes. It is built into DNA, ATP and cell membranes, and used in fertilizers.

name: Sulfur
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [32.059, 32.076]
summary: A yellow, brittle nonmetal found near volcanoes and in sulfide ores. It is a component of some amino acids and the source of sulfuric acid.

name: Chlorine
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [35.446, 35.457]
summary: A greenish-yellow, toxic gas that is strongly oxidizing. As chloride it is the main anion in seawater and body fluids, and it disinfects water.

name: Argon
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [39.792, 39.963]
summary: The third most abundant gas in air, about 1% by volume, and almost completely unreactive. It is used to shield welds from oxygen and to fill light bulbs.

name: Potassium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A soft alkali metal that reacts violently with water. Its ion is crucial for nerve function and plant growth, and it is a main fertilizer component.

name: Calcium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 4
summary: A silvery alkaline-earth metal that makes up bones, teeth and shells, and limestone rock. Its ion also acts as an important cellular signal.

name: Scandium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 4
summary: A light, silvery transition metal that is rare and widely dispersed. A small amount strengthens aluminum alloys for aerospace and sports gear.

name: Titanium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A strong, light, corrosion-resistant metal that is common in rocks. It is used in aircraft, implants and white pigment as titanium dioxide.

name: Vanadium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A hard, silvery-gray metal that forms colorful compounds in several oxidation states. Mostly added to steel to make it tougher.

name: Chromium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 6
summary: A hard, shiny metal that resists corrosion. It gives stainless steel its stainless character and provides chrome plating and green and red pigments.

name: Manganese
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A brittle gray-pink metal that is crucial for making steel. It also acts as a trace nutrient and appears in dry-cell batteries.

name: Iron
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: The most commonly used metal, magnetic and forming the core of Earth. It is the key atom in hemoglobin and the main component of steel.

name: Cobalt
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
discovered_note: Georg Brandt showed the blue colour of cobalt glass came from a new metal.
summary: A hard, blue-tinted magnetic metal. Used in alloys, battery cathodes and deep-blue pigments, and it sits at the center of vitamin B12.

name: Nickel
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 4
summary: A silvery, corrosion-resistant, magnetic metal. It appears in stainless steel, coins and rechargeable batteries, and is thought to be abundant in Earth's core.

name: Copper
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A reddish metal that conducts heat and electricity very well. It has been used since antiquity in wire, pipes and bronze.

name: Zinc
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A bluish-white metal that protects steel from rust as a coating. It is essential in many enzymes and is a component of brass.

name: Gallium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A soft metal that melts just above room temperature, so it liquefies in the hand. Its compounds power LEDs and high-speed electronics.

name: Germanium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 8
summary: A brittle, shiny metalloid and semiconductor that was used in the first transistors. Today it features in fiber optics and infrared optics.

name: Arsenic
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 6
summary: A metalloid known for its toxic compounds, which exist in gray, yellow and black forms. In semiconductors it is combined with gallium as gallium arsenide.

name: Selenium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 8
summary: A nonmetal related to sulfur that is both an essential trace nutrient and toxic in excess. It is used in glass, solar cells and photocopiers.

name: Bromine
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [79.901, 79.907]
summary: A dense, red-brown liquid that gives off irritating fumes, one of only two liquid elements at room temperature. Used in flame retardants and chemical synthesis.

name: Krypton
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A colorless, dense noble gas that is nearly inert. It emits bright lines of light in discharge lamps and was once used to define the meter.

name: Rubidium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A very reactive, soft alkali metal that melts a little above room temperature. It is used in atomic clocks and research.

name: Strontium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A soft alkaline-earth metal whose salts burn bright red in fireworks. It is chemically similar to calcium and gets deposited in bone.

name: Yttrium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
discovered_note: Johan Gadolin found yttrium oxide in a mineral; the metal was isolated later.
summary: A silvery metal usually found with the rare earths. Its compounds serve as red phosphors and in lasers and superconductors.

name: Zirconium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A strong, corrosion-resistant metal that barely absorbs neutrons, which suits it for nuclear fuel cladding. Zirconia crystals are used in ceramics and as a diamond simulant.

name: Niobium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A soft, gray, ductile metal that resists corrosion. Mostly alloyed in steel and used in superconducting magnets.

name: Molybdenum
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A hard metal with a very high melting point. Alloyed in steel for strength, and it is an active part of some enzymes.

name: Technetium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Tc-97 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: The lightest element with no stable isotopes, first made artificially. A metastable isotope is widely used in medical imaging.

name: Ruthenium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A hard, rare platinum-group metal. Used to harden alloys and in catalysts and electrical contacts.

name: Rhodium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A rare, silvery platinum-group metal that is very reflective and corrosion-resistant. Its main use is in automotive catalytic converters.

name: Palladium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A platinum-group metal that absorbs large volumes of hydrogen. Used heavily in catalytic converters and chemical catalysis.

name: Silver
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A shiny white metal with the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of any element. It is used in jewelry, coins, mirrors and photography.

name: Cadmium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 4
summary: A soft, bluish metal and toxic. Used in rechargeable batteries and pigments, though its use is being phased out.

name: Indium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A very soft, silvery metal that gives a cry when bent. Indium tin oxide forms the clear conductive coating on touchscreens.

name: Tin
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 7
summary: A soft, silvery metal that resists corrosion. Alloyed with copper to make bronze and used to coat steel cans and in solder.

name: Antimony
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A brittle, silvery metalloid. Mixed into alloys to harden them, and its compounds are used as flame retardants.

name: Tellurium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A brittle metalloid with a silvery luster that is related to sulfur. It is used in thermoelectric devices and solar panels made of cadmium telluride.

name: Iodine
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A dark-violet solid that sublimes into purple vapor. Essential for thyroid hormones and used as an antiseptic.

name: Xenon
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 6
summary: A heavy, colorless noble gas that glows bright blue-white in lamps. It is used as a medical anesthetic and in ion thrusters.

name: Cesium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 6
summary: A very soft, golden alkali metal that reacts explosively with water. Its atoms define the second in atomic clocks.

name: Barium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 7
summary: A soft, silvery-white alkaline-earth metal that is quite dense. Barium sulfate is used in X-ray imaging of the gut and gives fireworks a green flame.

name: Lanthanum
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 7
summary: A soft, silvery metal that starts off the lanthanide series. It is used in camera lenses, hybrid car batteries and lighter flints.

name: Cerium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: The most abundant rare-earth element, a gray metal that oxidizes easily. Ceria polishes glass and helps clean exhaust in catalytic converters.

name: Praseodymium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A soft, silvery rare-earth metal whose salts are green. Used in strong magnets and yellow-tinted glass.

name: Neodymium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
discovered_note: Mosander found 'didymium'; Auer von Welsbach split it into neodymium and praseodymium later.
summary: A rare-earth metal that is a key ingredient in the strongest permanent magnets. Also found in some lasers and in colored glass.

name: Promethium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Pm-145 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A radioactive rare earth with no stable isotope, so it is vanishingly rare in nature. It is used in some luminous paints and atomic batteries.

name: Samarium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A rare-earth metal. Samarium-cobalt magnets keep strength at high temperature, and one isotope is used in cancer pain treatment.

name: Europium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A soft rare-earth metal that is quite reactive. Its compounds glow red and blue, as in euro banknote security inks and television phosphors.

name: Gadolinium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A silvery rare-earth metal that is strongly magnetic near room temperature. Its compounds serve as contrast agents in MRI.

name: Terbium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 7
summary: A rare-earth metal whose compounds glow green. Used in solid-state devices, fluorescent lamps and magnetostrictive alloys.

name: Dysprosium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A rare-earth metal with a very strong magnetic response. Added to high-performance magnets and used in nuclear control rods.

name: Holmium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 5
summary: A rare-earth metal with the highest magnetic moment of any element. Used in lasers and to focus magnetic fields.

name: Erbium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A rare-earth metal with pink compounds. Doped into optical fibers to amplify signals and used in medical lasers.

name: Thulium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 5
summary: A rare lanthanide that is among the least abundant of the rare earths. Used in some portable X-ray sources and certain lasers.

name: Ytterbium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 10
summary: A soft rare-earth metal. Used in precise atomic clocks, fiber lasers and as an X-ray source.

name: Lutetium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 5
summary: The densest and hardest lanthanide, the last in its series. Used in specialized catalysts and PET detectors.

name: Hafnium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 6
summary: A dense, ductile metal that so closely resembles zirconium it was hard to isolate. It absorbs neutrons well and appears in nuclear reactor control rods and chip insulators.

name: Tantalum
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A dense, gray, very corrosion-resistant metal. Its main use is in tiny capacitors for phones and computers, and in surgical implants.

name: Tungsten
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A very dense metal with the highest melting point of all metals. Used in light bulb filaments, cutting tools and armor-piercing parts.

name: Rhenium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A very rare, extremely dense metal with the second highest melting point of all elements. It improves superalloys for jet engines and is used in catalysts.

name: Osmium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: One of the two densest elements (with iridium), a bluish-white, brittle metal. It is alloyed into hard-wearing pen tips and electrical contacts.

name: Iridium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 2
summary: A very dense, brittle, corrosion-resistant metal and very rare in Earth's crust. A thin layer rich in iridium in rocks worldwide marks the asteroid impact that ended the age of the dinosaurs.

name: Platinum
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 9
summary: A dense, noble, corrosion-resistant metal. Used as a catalyst in cars and industry, in jewelry, and in some cancer drugs.

name: Gold
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 4
summary: A dense, soft, yellow metal that does not tarnish. Valued as jewelry, currency and in electronics contacts.

name: Mercury
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A dense, silvery metal that is liquid at room temperature and highly toxic. It was once used in thermometers and barometers.

name: Thallium
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [204.382, 204.385]
summary: A soft, heavy metal whose compounds are highly toxic. It was used in rat poisons and today in specialty glass and optics.

name: Lead
mass_note: CIAAW conventional (abridged) value; the true value varies between sources, CIAAW interval [206.14, 207.94]
summary: A heavy, soft, bluish metal with a low melting point. Once common in pipes, paint and gasoline, but toxic; used in batteries and radiation shielding.

name: Bismuth
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
summary: A brittle, heavy, pinkish metal with surprisingly low toxicity. It forms colorful oxidized films, and it is used in pigments and medicines.

name: Polonium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Po-209 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A rare, intensely radioactive metal discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie, who named it for Marie's homeland, Poland. It occurs in tiny traces in uranium ores.

name: Astatine
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, At-210 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: The rarest naturally occurring element, intensely radioactive and short-lived. Tiny quantities are made in labs for studying halogen chemistry.

name: Radon
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Rn-222 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
discovered_note: Rutherford and Owens found the gas; Dorn's isotope gave radon its name.
summary: A dense radioactive noble gas produced by the decay of radium in rocks. It can accumulate in basements and is a lung cancer hazard.

name: Francium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Fr-223 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: An extremely rare, highly unstable alkali metal. Its longest-lived isotope lasts only about 22 minutes.

name: Radium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Ra-226 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A radioactive alkaline-earth metal that glows faintly. Discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie, it was used in luminous paint and early cancer treatments.

name: Actinium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Ac-227 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A radioactive, silvery metal that gives its name to the actinide series. Its isotopes are found in trace amounts in uranium ores.

name: Thorium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 4
summary: A weakly radioactive, silvery metal found in many rocks and sands. Its isotope thorium-232 lives so long that it is one of the few heavy radioactive elements still around from before the Earth formed, and it has been studied as a nuclear fuel.

name: Protactinium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 1
discovered_note: Fajans and Goehring found a short-lived isotope; Hahn and Meitner found the longer-lived Pa-231 in 1918.
summary: A rare, dense, radioactive metal found in uranium ore. Chemically it is hard to work with, and it has few uses.

name: Uranium
mass_note: CIAAW standard atomic weight, uncertainty in last digit(s): 3
summary: A heavy, weakly radioactive metal that is the main fuel for nuclear reactors. Natural uranium is mostly the isotope 238, with a small fraction of fissile uranium-235.

name: Neptunium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Np-237 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: The first transuranic element, made by neutron capture in uranium. Its longest-lived isotope appears as a long-lived component in spent nuclear fuel.

name: Plutonium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Pu-244 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A heavy radioactive metal produced in reactors from uranium. It fuels some reactors and weapons, and powers deep-space probes through its decay heat.

name: Americium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Am-243 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A radioactive metal made in reactors. Its isotope americium-241 is used in common smoke detectors.

name: Curium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Cm-247 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A synthetic radioactive metal named after Marie and Pierre Curie. Its isotopes have been used as power sources and in X-ray spectrometers on space probes.

name: Berkelium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Bk-247 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A synthetic radioactive element first made in Berkeley, California. It is produced in research reactors in tiny amounts and used to make heavier elements.

name: Californium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Cf-251 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A synthetic radioactive element that is a strong neutron emitter. Used as a neutron source for starting reactors and in cancer therapy.

name: Einsteinium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Es-252 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A synthetic radioactive element first found in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test. Only tiny amounts have ever been made.

name: Fermium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Fm-257 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A synthetic radioactive element also first identified in hydrogen bomb fallout. It can only be made in minuscule quantities.

name: Mendelevium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Md-258 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A synthetic radioactive element, named after the creator of the periodic table, made one atom at a time in early experiments.

name: Nobelium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, No-259 (NUBASE2020 mass excess)
summary: A synthetic radioactive element made in particle accelerators. Studied in minute quantities, with its chemistry mostly like ytterbium.

name: Lawrencium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Lr-266 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
summary: The last of the actinides, a synthetic radioactive element with short-lived isotopes. Only a few atoms at a time have been studied.

name: Rutherfordium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Rf-267 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
discovered_note: Claimed in Russia in 1964 and at Berkeley in 1969.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element and the first of the transactinides. It has been made only in accelerators, and its isotopes are short-lived.

name: Dubnium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Db-268 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
discovered_note: Claimed in Russia in 1968 and at Berkeley in 1970.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element made in accelerators, with short-lived isotopes. It sits below tantalum, and the few atoms studied behave like its group-5 neighbours niobium and tantalum.

name: Seaborgium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Sg-269 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element with short-lived isotopes. The few compounds studied behave like those of its lighter neighbours molybdenum and tungsten.

name: Bohrium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Bh-270 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element produced only a few atoms at a time. Chemical tests show it to be like rhenium.

name: Hassium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Hs-269 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element with a volatile oxide, studied one atom at a time. It sits below osmium in the periodic table.

name: Meitnerium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Mt-277 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element with very short-lived isotopes. Expected to be a dense metal like iridium.

name: Darmstadtium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Ds-282 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here. Calculations disagree: the CRC Handbook gives 6d9 7s1.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element made in accelerators, a few atoms at a time. Its longest-lived known isotope has a half-life of only minutes, and most last far less.

name: Roentgenium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Rg-282 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here. Calculations disagree: the CRC Handbook gives 6d10 7s1.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element, made by fusing nickel and bismuth. Expected to be a metal like gold.

name: Copernicium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Cn-285 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element that may behave as a volatile metal, possibly a gas at room temperature, as its chemistry is studied atom by atom.

name: Nihonium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Nh-286 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
discovered_note: Detected in Russia in 2003 and at RIKEN (Japan) in 2004; recognised in 2015.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element first synthesized in Japan and Russia. Only a handful of atoms with very short half-lives have been seen.

name: Flerovium
mass_note: No stable isotopes: mass of the longest-lived isotope, Fl-290 (NUBASE2020 mass excess); extrapolated
config_note: Not measured spectroscopically; NIST (Z<=108) or the cited prediction (Z>=109). Relativistic effects are large here.
summary: A synthetic superheavy element whose chemistry has been probed with a few atoms. It may be volatile and relatively unreactive.

name: Moscovium
